title: What a Concurrence Is For
hook: A concurring justice agrees with the outcome — and sometimes uses the space to propose demolishing the doctrine the majority just applied. Today's lone concurrence is tomorrow's majority.
key_points: A concurrence agrees with the Court's result; some add almost nothing, others urge a major change in the law.
Chemerinsky flags Kagan in Chiles v. Salazar, suggesting subject-matter speech restrictions may not require strict scrutiny.
Gorsuch in Chatrie v. United States would scrap the 60-year-old 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test for a property-based one.
Thomas in Monsanto v. Durnell questioned Commerce Clause reach, delegated legislative power, and agency preemption at once.
Kavanaugh's birthright-citizenship concurrence in Trump v. Barbara reads, in Chemerinsky's view, like living-constitution reasoning.
Concurrences matter because a future majority can adopt them — read them as proposals, not footnotes.
content_html: When a justice agrees with how a case comes out, why write separately at all? Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of UC Berkeley School of Law, argues that concurrences are wildly uneven: some "add little to what is in the court's decision," while others take a very different route and press for a major change in the law. The second kind is worth reading closely, because concurrences are how doctrinal shifts get proposed before they get adopted.
extra_html:
His examples from the term show the range. Justice Kagan, concurring in Chiles v. Salazar on conversion therapy, suggested that restrictions on a subject of speech — unlike restrictions on a viewpoint — might not trigger strict scrutiny; Chemerinsky warns that would substantially lower the Constitution's protection for speech. Justice Gorsuch, in the geofence-search case Chatrie v. United States, would discard the roughly six-decade-old "reasonable expectation of privacy" framework and ground Fourth Amendment protection in personal property rights instead. Justice Thomas, concurring in the pesticide-preemption case Monsanto Co. v. Durnell, raised doubts about Congress's Commerce Clause authority, delegated legislative power, and agency preemption — three threads that, pulled together, would put a great deal of existing federal law in question. And Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence in the birthright-citizenship case Trump v. Barbara struck Chemerinsky as living-constitution reasoning from a professed originalist.

None of these opinions changed the law. That is the point. A concurrence is a low-cost way to put an idea into circulation and wait for four more votes, which is why experienced readers of any court treat separate opinions as a forecast rather than a footnote.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

related.title: The Power of a Dissent
related.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

related.title: Geofence Warrants & the Fourth Amendment
related.hook: Police can ask a tech company which phones were near a crime scene at a given hour — sweeping up everyone's location, not just a suspect's. In 2026 the Court said that's a 'search.'

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

flashcards.prompt: What is a concurring opinion, and why can it matter more than the vote it adds?
flashcards.back_html: An opinion by a justice who agrees with the Court's result but writes separately. It adds no votes, but it can float a doctrinal change that a later majority picks up.

flashcards.prompt: In Chemerinsky's account, what would Gorsuch's Chatrie concurrence change about the Fourth Amendment?

choices.text: Replace the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test with one based on personal property rights
Require a warrant for every search, with no exceptions
Remove the Fourth Amendment's application to digital records entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: Gorsuch would discard the roughly 60-year-old expectation-of-privacy test in favor of property rights — an approach Chemerinsky argues would lessen privacy protection.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Chemerinsky treat some concurrences as warnings rather than commentary?

choices.text: Because they propose overhauls — of speech doctrine, the Commerce Clause, preemption — that a future majority could adopt
Because a concurrence overrides the majority opinion in later cases
Because concurrences are binding on lower courts

flashcards.explanation_html: They are not binding, but they map out where doctrine could go. Several this term would unsettle large bodies of existing federal law if adopted.
